prize_parts.citation: for developing empirical methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets

statement.case_for: Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices turned differentiated-product markets into something that can be measured. Merger review, antitrust, regulation, trade, health and environmental policy all use the framework routinely, so its reach goes well beyond IO. This is the breadth-of-use criterion I would apply to any field. The core is a joint contribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995). Pakes' dynamic-industry and estimation work adds depth. The methods are three decades old and have been tested, extended and criticised. Colleagues' openings broadly agree on the BLP core. After reading them, I move my opening third name from Bresnahan to Levinsohn, because a citation about demand estimation should credit all three authors of the paper it rests on.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a methods prize with no single headline empirical finding. The three-name limit also excludes Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, who made important contributions to the wider New Empirical IO tradition. Results from BLP-type estimators can be sensitive to instruments, functional form and implementation. The committee may judge that a toolkit ranks below a substantive discovery such as firm heterogeneity or the labour-market effects of trade and technology.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B005 first, calls the BLP demand-estimation contribution cleanly attributable to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, and asks whether Bresnahan or Reiss should be preferred over Levinsohn.
responses.response: I agree on attribution and have revised my opening, where I had Bresnahan in place of Levinsohn. Bresnahan's work on inferring market power is a precursor of the BLP approach, but it is a different contribution from the one the citation would reward. A three-person prize naming demand estimation should credit the three authors of the paper that delivered it. I share the concern about a methods prize. I would answer it by pointing to the policy and cross-field use, not by widening the credit set to include Bresnahan or Reiss.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B005 eighth. He sees the credit set as large and diffuse and flags sensitivity of BLP estimates to implementation and instruments, and whether this is a methodological contribution rather than a discovery.
responses.response: The diffuseness is real on the seven-name ballot, but the problem goes away once the citation is limited to demand and competition in differentiated-product markets. That set has a clear anchor in one jointly authored paper and its direct extensions. I accept that implementation sensitivity is a genuine concern. I would argue it shows how far the method has been used and scrutinised, as with other widely adopted empirical tools, and does not undermine it. I do not accept that a method cannot be a scientific discovery here, because it changed what questions about market power and welfare can be answered with data.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B014 first. He argues that Persson, Tabellini and Besley gave a unified theoretical and empirical framework for how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape policy, and he notes possible overlap with the 2024 institutions prize.
responses.response: I see B014 as a strong, mature programme, and I accept that it opened a field. My reservations are that causal identification from cross-country constitutional variation is weaker than in design-based or structural work, and that the 2024 prize on institutions weakens the case for novelty. This is a qualification, not a rejection. I would want a more detailed discussion of which results are well identified and how far the Persson-Tabellini and Besley strands are one achievement. On the evidence in the openings, I still weigh breadth of use across other fields more heavily, which favours B005.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would rather frame an IO prize around the broader New Empirical IO tradition, which would bring Bresnahan back in, than around the demand-estimation core.
How much weight to give a methods contribution relative to substantive discoveries such as B025 and B030, and whether recent prizes on identification and causal methods affect the margin.
How sensitive BLP-type estimates are to implementation and instruments, and how far that should qualify the case.
Whether B025 should rank higher once the credit relative to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on that ballot, is weighed.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any candidate on the shortlist is apparent from the supplied profile. I do disclose that my own research is in industrial organization and pricing, so I may be inclined to favour B005, and I rely on cross-field use as the common criterion. I have co-authored with committee colleagues John Hassler and Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026). That bears on committee relationships, not on any candidate. The profile also records that I am married to a former Swedish prime minister, which is a public fact with no apparent bearing on this ballot.
